feature_title: 2026 college football win totals I'm betting now
author: Steve Makinen
stated_method: going back through the coaching changes, the Stability Scores, the transitional systems, the recruiting rankings, and playing out the schedule by his power ratings

entries.text: The Broncos +1.7 difference represents one of the biggest I’ve ever had in projecting wins against the schedule using my power ratings, and I even double- and triple-checked the numbers to be sure. I think the oddsmakers are giving a bit too much credit to the strength of the new Pac-12, and in my opinion, BSU is the obvious favorite. QB Maddux Madsen returns as a senior, and head coach Spencer Danielson is in his fourth year with the program. With the opener at Oregon the only likely loss I see on the 2026 slate, I think Boise takes the newly formed Pac-12 and exceeds the modest win total of 7.5. I’d probably even be willing to bet it up to at least 8.5.

Fresno State surprised me last season by exceeding expectations in head coach Matt Entz’s first year. Sometimes it takes a coach a bit of time to find his footing. In terms of FSU football, Entz did not, as his team finished 9-4. He responded to that success by adding an extremely improved recruiting class as graded by 247Sports. Considering the Bulldogs’ success last year, and now transitioning into the remade Pac- 12, the future looks bright for Entz & Co. With 13 starters back, they also qualify for a unique transition system, indicating that of the 141 teams over the last five years that brought back at least four starters more than the prior season, only 40 got worse. The average improvement of the group that didn’t drop off was a winning percentage bump of 15% (+3.2 wins) and ATS rise of 6.7%.

Second-year head coach Zach Kittley’s first team at Florida Atlantic was, if nothing else, fun to watch. The Owls had the most offensive plays per game and the most passing yards per game in the country last year. However, they also led the nation in giveaways. Now, with a year in the new system under their belt, I see a lot of reasons for potential improvement. QB Caden Veltkamp is back for his senior year after throwing for over 3,600 yards last season, along with 11 other starters. FAU qualifies for three different transition angles as well. 1) Over the last five seasons, there have been 18 teams that managed to go .500 or better against the spread despite having a -0.8 or worse turnover differential per game. Of those teams, only four regressed in the follow-up campaign, and the average improvement for the entire group was 8.7% SU while winning 1.4 more games on average. 2) In the “there’s nowhere to go but up” category, since 2021, there have been 21 teams that have won four or fewer games in a season while enduring a -0.8 or worse turnover ratio. Only two of those 21 teams regressed. The average win improvement for the other 19 teams was 2.3 per season, and the SU win % upgrade was 15.3%. 3) Of the 141 teams over the last five years that brought back at least four starters more than the prior season, only 40 got worse. The average improvement of the group that didn’t drop off was a winning percentage bump of 15% (+3.2 wins) and ATS rise of 6.7%. With a lot of American Conference teams facing questions this season, I think this has the chance to be FAU’s best football year since the Lane Kiffin days.

The move to the Big 12 has helped Houston put together its best five- year recruiting classes on record. Under head coach Willie Fritz, a new, consistent standard is being established. Last season, this team won nine games in the regular season and then beat LSU in a thrilling Texas Bowl game. QB Conner Weigman, a former A&M transfer, had a huge year for the Cougars and is back for his senior season. In all, there are 19 starters back, making Houston one of two teams with a Stability Score of 18 on my scale, with Notre Dame being the other. It should also be noted that teams returning 17+ starters have combined to go 55.7% ATS in the first four weeks of the last five college football seasons, meaning this program should be able to carry over the momentum of last year’s solid finish. Plus, of the 141 teams over the last five years that brought back at least four starters more than the prior season, only 40 got worse. The average improvement of the group that didn’t drop off was a winning percentage bump of 15% (+3.2 wins) and ATS rise of 6.7%. This should be a big year for Fritz & Co.

After getting a winner with the Illini last year on their Over win total prop, I’m going back to the well in 2026. Fifth-year coach Bret Bielema brought in another solid recruiting class this spring, best on record, in fact, and it’s clear that this program is reaping the benefits of winning on the field. Bielema’s group has won 19 games over the last two seasons and has improved from a Big Ten bottom-feeder as far as recruiting is concerned to a mid-level destination. To me, it seems obvious that this program has turned a corner and is here to stay. They do lose QB Luke Altmyer, but replacing him is another former Big Ten starter, Katin Houser from Michigan State. There are 11 other starters in place. The Illini do face Ohio State and Oregon, but in all honesty, it’s hard to see them as a likely loser in any other game. by Steve Makinen 23

It came as a bit of a shock for KSU fans when Chris Klieman announced his retirement as head football coach in December. He stepped away citing personal health and family considerations and did it with the Wildcats coming off a 6-6 season, but also with a reasonable amount of starting experience coming back. Leading that charge is third-year starting QB Avery Johnson. In Klieman’s place steps Collin Klein, who gets his first head coaching gig after spending seven seasons in Manhattan as an offensive assistant before serving as Texas A&M’s OC the last two years. As I look at last season, KSU was so close to bigger successes, but suffered five of its six losses by six points or fewer. That, combined with Johnson returning as a senior, makes this an ideal situation for Klein to step in and have some immediate positive impact. He played at KSU from 2008-12 so already has a tremendous bond with the program, and his hiring was met with a lot of optimism. With no Texas Tech or BYU on the 2026 slate, I think this team has an outside shot at contending for a Big 12 title game berth.

Sometimes, there’s no rhyme or reason to figuring out why a specific improvement or decline in a recruiting season occurs. I don’t think South Alabama fans care about the how or why here, but in his third season, coming off a disappointing 4-8 record, head coach Major Applewhite was able to secure his best recruit/transfer class this spring, with the 86th ranking beating last year’s grade by 31 positions. Several of the newcomers are P4 transfers. It gives USA at least a shot at getting a lot better on the field this fall. Also encouraging is the fact that QB Bishop Davenport is back for his senior season after leading this team to 26.5 PPG last year. The Sun Belt Conference doesn’t have a lot of teams contending for the role of favorite this season, and the Jaguars’ conference slate is mild at best. I like this team to return to a bowl game this fall.

South Carolina dropped by five wins in the regular season last year, and quite honestly, it was unexpected. The Gamecocks lost four games by 10 points or less, all against teams that were ranked in the Top 25 at the time. Fortunately for head coach Shane Beamer, many of the key players decided to steady the ship and come back for another run, including QB LaNorris Sellers, this team’s offensive star. This is another team with several key transition systems to consider, among them: 1) One of the biggest improvements in wins from one season to the next you’ll find comes when nine or more offensive starters, including the quarterback, return from a team that won 50% or less of its games outright in the prior season. The average win increase is +2.7 wins & 13.3% SU. 2) There have been 43 teams over the last five seasons that have endured losing seasons despite outscoring their opponents. Of those, 17 of them brought back 13 or more starters, including their quarterback. The collective improvement of this group of teams was about 20% SU (+3.4 wins) and 8.9% ATS. These teams combined to go 56.5% ATS, a profit- making collection. Beamer’s team has a realistic shot of heading to Florida in October with a 4-1 record at least. A win there would give this team a ton of momentum in returning to where they were two years ago.

There are a lot of reasons why teams can yo-yo from one season to the next nowadays in college football. Losing a lot of key players from a successful team the prior year is at the head of the list in terms of why teams might drop. That clearly affected Syracuse in 2025, as the Orange went from 10-3 to 3-9. Turnovers can also be big, and they were for ‘Cuse last season. However, in the “there’s nowhere to go but up” category, since 2021, there have been 21 teams that have won four or fewer games in a season while enduring a -0.8 or worse turnover ratio. Only two of those 21 teams regressed. The average win improvement for the other 19 teams was 2.3 per season, and the SU win % upgrade was 15.3%. Overall, recruiting at Syracuse has seen an upgrade under Fran Brown, who begins his third season with the program. He is obviously a pretty strong salesman, as he was able to land the second-highest-rated class the Orange have seen in the last 17 years, despite coming off a 3-9 record. With QB Steve Angeli back for his senior season, and the ACC looking down for 2026, I think the Orange have a good chance to rebound.

The pressure on Texas and QB Arch Manning last year was palpable; you could sense it every time they took the field. Expectations were beyond reasonable control. The fact that the Longhorns still won 10 games despite a 5-7-1 ATS record shows just how much even the experts behind the bookmaking counter thought of this group. Well, they say that all is well that ends well, and head coach Steve Sarkisian’s team won its final three games of 2025, and Manning exploded statistically in those contests. The offense put up 456 yards in the bowl win over Michigan. That is the momentum they will be carrying into 2026. In addition, a program that achieved its first-ever No. 1 recruiting ranking in the country on record last year, then followed it up with a No. 3 rank, seems due for lofty goals. There is one key transitional system I have my eye on regarding Texas: Only three of the last 33 teams since 2021 that had nine or more offensive returning starters, including the quarterback, from a team that won 45% or less of its games against the spread in the prior season, got worse. The average win increase of the other 30 teams was +2.0 wins, 6.7% SU, and 16.8% ATS. These teams were also about 53% ATS. Two additional wins would put this team at 11-1. I think that’s realistic with the talent that is in place here and a QB 100% ready to fulfill his immense promise.

VSiN college football fans will know that I throw the term “stability” around often, particularly in the offseason. One of the more stable teams prepping for 2026 across the country is head coach Mike Elko’s Texas A&M squad, a team that reached the CFP last year but was stymied by Miami at home. With Elko in his third year now in College Station, I think last year’s growth of three wins will prove to be a big stepping stone forward for the program into elite territory. QB Marcel Reed returns again for the Aggies as a junior, along with 17 other starters! Teams returning a starting quarterback for at least a second straight season as a starter usually show nice improvement, typically by about 0.9 wins per season (+1.4% win pct). When you add the same head coach/offensive coordinator to the recipe along with at least seven other total offensive returning starters, the improvement jumps by 1.3 wins per season and 53.3% ATS combined, a profitable group. Of the 38 teams, only 12 won fewer games. Similarly, only three of the last 33 teams since 2021 that had nine or more offensive returning starters, including the quarterback, from a team that won 45% or less of its games against the spread in the prior season, got worse. The average win increase of the other 30 teams was +2.0 wins, 6.7% SU, and 16.8% ATS. These teams were also about 53% ATS. As I said earlier… very stable situation here, and a very talented roster and coaching staff. That’s usually a great combination. Marcel Reed

After guiding James Madison to the CFP last season, a lot of power conference schools had interest in Bob Chesney, and he eventually settled at UCLA, where he takes over for DeShaun Foster, who guided the Bruins through two seasons of 8-16 football. The 2025 UCLA team was a massive disappointment, particularly after landing QB Nico Iamaleava in the transfer portal. Nico was a lightning rod for the program and was vilified when the team struggled and praised during the shocking three-game Big Ten winning streak in October. Chesney does get Iamaleava back for 2026, plus numerous Power Four starters in as transfers. In all, this program is expected to have what amounts to 18 starting players filling spots for this fall, a lofty number in this day and age. Clearly there is major room for improvement when a team wins less than 50% of its games in the prior season, but some of the biggest improvement is realized when these teams bring back their starting quarterback plus hire a new head coach and coordinators. Over the last five seasons, the average winning percentage increase of the 21 teams that have done this has been 15.2% SU (+2.1 wins) and 13.3% ATS. Only one of the 21 teams got worse. Will it amount to winning on the field this season? Well, the schedule has what I would consider to be six very winnable home games, and the win total is only 6.5 at DraftKings. I think this situation has a good chance of surpassing that number, and there will be an obvious coaching upgrade.

Do yourself a favor…go through the UNLV schedule for 2026, which is minus Boise State this year after the Broncos left for the Pac-12, and tell me if there are any games which you designate in the “likely loss” category. In my opinion, with the meteoric rise New Mexico made last year, the Runnin’ Rebels’ Mountain West consistency in recent years makes them the favorite in the league. Including Auburn transfer QB Jackson Arnold, UNLV Head Coach Dan Mullen seems to have picked up right where successful prior coach Barry Odom left off, bringing in highly-respected recruiting classes to carry on the momentum of 30-12 over the past three years. Mullen has been able to bring in numerous P4 transfers with the allure of Sin City. This should have the Runnin’ Rebels in the hunt for MWC titles year-in and year-out for the near future. Running this team’s power rating against the 2026 schedule produced a 9-3 record. The most balanced wagering option at DK on the win total sits at a modest 7.5. I would have no problem betting it upward either.

Though James Franklin had very good success at Penn State, his teams could never meet the demands of the fans in Happy Valley. That said, he was perhaps never as effusive in his praise of his team’s offseason work as he has been this season. The excitement for Hokies’ football is palpable, mostly because of the eagerness Franklin is showing to get things started. He was able to retain 15 of this team’s starters from last year and added three more through the portal, including PSU QB Ethan Grunkemeyer, who started seven games as a freshman last year. There are two nice transitional angles backing the Hokies for improvement in 2026: 1) Of the 141 teams over the last five years that brought back at least four starters more than the prior season, only 40 got worse. The average improvement of the group that didn’t drop off was a winning percentage bump of 15% (+3.2 wins) and an ATS rise of 6.7%. 2) In the “there’s nowhere to go but up” category, since 2021, there have been 21 teams that have won four or fewer games in a season while enduring a -0.8 or worse turnover ratio. Only 2 of those 21 teams regressed. The average win improvement for the other 19 teams was 2.3 per season, and the SU win % upgrade was 15.3%. With the upgraded coaching staff, the vast experience returning, and the overall excitement peaking, DK has posted a win total of about 6.5, which to me seems a little understated in a season of a lot of question marks in the ACC. There are some very probable wins early on the schedule, which could propel this team to a very nice 2026 season. 15 teams I project to go Under their DraftKings season win props

Is there cause for concern already in Myrtle Beach as new head coach Ryan Beard begins his tenure with the Coastal Carolina program? The Chanticleers have been a bowl-game fixture and Sun Belt contender over the last half-decade or so. His first recruiting class was a nightmare by program standards, this coming on the heels of what is a sliding performance chart. Beard’s predecessor Tim Beck failed to live up to the successes of his predecessor Jamey Chadwell and was eventually fired at the conclusion of the 6-6 regular season last year. His swan song was a 59-10 drubbing at the hands of James Madison. The program followed that up with another bowl game loss. In the final three regular season games, Beck’s CCU team was outscored 155-57. Thus, the Chanticleers will be looking to snap a four-game losing skid in their opener at West Virginia. There is a junior college transfer QB sitting No. 1 on the depth chart right now in Tre Guerra, and very little starting experience coming back elsewhere. The win total is at 4.5, a very low number considering where this program has been in recent years. I think the experts are telling us this is going to be a trying season in Myrtle Beach.

New head coach Jason Candle spent a decade at Toledo, and it was a very successful run, as he went 81-44 and the Rockets finished at least .500 in every season. He gets the chance to keep the momentum going at UConn. Here the Huskies come off back-to-back nine-win seasons under former coach Jim Mora, Jr. Candle’s experience and past successes alone might not be enough this season, as he will have one of the most inexperienced rosters in the country and the schedule is a bit tougher than we’ve been accustomed to with UConn under Mora. Oddsmakers are, in fact, expecting a pretty sharp drop-off this season in Storrs, as UConn’s win total is set at a mere 5.5 after the recent run of success. With three Power Four schools on the schedule and a handful of other prominent G5 programs, I think we’re going to see some first-year struggles for Candle & Co. If it’s data you are hoping for besides the zero stability rating, consider that teams that are off of seasons in which they won 60% or more of their games outright and have four or fewer offensive starters returning, plus are breaking in a new quarterback Nico Iamaleava have dropped by an average of -3.7 wins, -26% outright, -11.7% ATS, and -6.6 PPG offensively. The eight teams that added a new head coach plummeted by 29% and -4.4 wins per season, and UConn fits the bill. If that weren’t enough, there is a potential landmine system that has affected teams coming off a season in which they enjoyed a positive 1.0 or better turnover differential but are now starting fresh at quarterback. The 27 most recent teams that have fit this bill over the last decade have dropped by 2.6 wins per season in the next campaign, representing a 18.5% plunge outright and 11.8% dip ATS.

Matt Campbell left quite an impression and lasting legacy at Iowa State in the decade he was in Ames. Unfortunately, when he opted to leave for Penn State, he also took a lot of his players he worked so hard to recruit to ISU with him. As a result, new head coach Jimmy Rogers, last out of Washington State, starts his first season here essentially from scratch. On the roster are only two players on each side of the ball with any FBS starting experience, and one is a transfer QB Jaylen Raynor from a Sun Belt program. It could be a very long year in Ames, and most respected prognosticators have this perennial contending program projected at the bottom of the Big 12. Of course, DraftKings’ oddsmakers don’t seem to be as much in a doom-and-gloom forecast mode for ISU as those trying to analyze the numbers. They have set the season win total for the Cyclones at 5.5, just 2.5 off of last year’s 8-4 season. If you recall, this program opted out of a bowl game after too many players transferred out. There are a couple of probable wins on the non-conference slate, but at this point, it’s hard to see ISU favored in any Big 12 game. Look at a couple of the data systems suggesting a Cyclones fall: 1) Over the last five years, 51 teams have had at least eight fewer returning starters than the prior season, and only 15 of them have improved that season. The average drop-off of those that didn’t improve was a winning percentage decline of 24% (-3.3 wins) and ATS drop of about 6.3%. 2) Teams that are off seasons in which they won 60% or more of their games outright and have four or fewer offensive starters returning, plus are breaking in a new quarterback, have dropped by an average of -3.7 wins, -26% outright, -11.7% ATS, and -6.6 PPG offensively. The eight teams that added a new head coach plummeted by 29% & -4.4 wins per season. I’m dead set on Under on this one, as a lot of conference rivals will be ready to pounce on a formerly prominent program in transition.

For Mark Stoops to last a decade in the SEC at perhaps the conference’s premier basketball school says a lot about the stability he brought to the Kentucky program. In all, he took the Wildcats to eight bowl games and won 82 games. His dismissal came after an embarrassing 41-0 season- ending loss to Louisville, as university brass decided it was time to move on. The new hire is a Louisville guy, as Will Stein played quarterback there for five years and started his coaching career there some 13 years ago. Since then, he has made a few stops, including most recently serving as offensive coordinator for Oregon. He led a high-powered offense there with QB Dante Moore, but there isn’t that type of talent right now at UK, nor has there been on that side of the ball for a long time. There is a lot of other transfer talent fresh to Lexington as well, but that might not make it any easier for the new regime in Year 1. The DK win total is a modest 4.5, and when looking at the schedule, it would still require an upset or two. It’s Arkansas or Kentucky for the bottom of the SEC this season. Let’s lean Under here.

To this day, I’ve always been puzzled as to why head coach Jamey Chadwell left Coastal Carolina and Myrtle Beach and opted for Liberty. I have felt that recruiting would naturally be tougher in Lynchburg, VA. Well, after a solid 2025 graded class came in and produced a 4-8 record, the 2026 class bottomed out by 34 ranking positions. I’m not sure the worst is behind the Flames, and I’m intrigued as to why oddsmakers would post a significantly improved win total of 8.5 after last year’s struggles, or why some respected prognosticators would have the Flames atop CUSA in the preseason? Plus, after three straight years of having the nation’s easiest schedule on paper, this year Liberty is sixth-easiest. This team might be better in 2026 than last year, but five games better? That seems like a stretch.

Charles Huff is making his third coaching stop in as many years after guiding Marshall and Southern Miss to successful seasons in 2024 and 2025. He makes a jump up this time to Memphis, where he takes over a program that has been one of the better and most consistent Group of Five teams for the last decade-plus. Like his predecessors at Memphis, including most recently Ryan Silverfield, you’d have to believe that this job is viewed as another step up the ladder for the oft-moving Huff. His name has become synonymous with instability, and unlike recent seasons, Memphis is not picked among the elite teams in the American Conference in 2026, sixth in fact by Phil Steele. There is only one 2025 Tigers’ starter back, so most of what you’ll see from this team will be totally fresh. There is a unique transitional angle in play for the Tigers here too: There have been 33 teams over the last six seasons that have recorded 4+ blowout wins of 20 points or more in one season, then had to change head coaches for one reason or another. Only five of the 33 teams got better the next season, and collectively, they dropped by an average of 17.2%, or 2.8 wins per season, as well as 11.4% ATS. As a group, they were 44.2% ATS. The inexperience will certainly be a factor, as will the supposed starting QB, after the spring game listed as Marcus Stokes, a transfer from D-2 Western Florida. This might be too big of a step up for Stokes and Huff.

It was a solid first season at the FBS level and in Conference USA for Missouri State as the Bears won seven games and received a bowl bid, a game they would eventually lose to Arkansas State. Year 2 at college football’s top level looks to be a little more challenging, however, as the program moves on from Ryan Beard, the head coach of the last three years, who led them through a very successful transition. Casey Woods, who last served as SMU’s offensive coordinator, takes the reins in his first chance as a head coach. He inherits a team with a Stability Score of zero for the season. There is very little experience on the roster, including at QB, where Duke transfer Henry Belin is expected to take over as a senior, and he is guiding a program that generally overachieved last season. Beating expectations by so much is a tough ask of any team. DraftKings sets the main win total line at 4.5. That might be overzealous, especially after a season in which the Bears won five games by seven points or fewer. Close wins are often characterized as getting “lucky” over the course of a season. Well, teams that have a lot of them and then come back inexperienced are naturally expected to drop. Over the last 13 seasons, 73 teams brought back 14 starters or fewer and had a new QB from a team that was fortunate to get four or more close wins of seven points or fewer in the prior season. Only 11 of these teams finished better the next season, with the average win drop being 2.6 per season, a 16.7% plunge.

Last year was supposed to be the year that head coach Matt Rhule and Nebraska took that elusive step forward. Or was it the year before? Or the year before that? Well, years of failing to live up to billing might have finally come crashing down on Nebraska and Rhule. His 2026 recruit/ transfer class ranked 66th in the country. Not only is that a severe drop- off from the program’s 15-year average, but it was the worst ranking the Cornhuskers have received in that time span by 31 positions. I can’t imagine this will help improve on back-to-back 7-6 seasons. Typically, when expectations fail to be met year in and year out, it is the problem of those setting the expectations, not the team. For this year, the season win prop is set at 6.5, similar to recent seasons seemingly without much consideration given to what personnel was lost or gained in the offseason. In my opinion, the Cornhuskers are down a bit, and the last seven weeks of the Big Ten slate are ridiculously tough. Let’s go Under on this one.

Talk about a challenging set of circumstances facing Rob Harley in 2026 for Northern Illinois. Not only is he a new head coach for the first time, he is also doing it under the tag of interim and is guiding a team that is in a transition year to a new and more challenging conference. It wasn’t like the team he is taking over was elite last year either. The Huskies finished 3-9 for former coach Thomas Hammock. I don’t know exactly what the most optimistic NIU fans are hoping for this fall, but it’s probably too much. The Phil Steele guide shows NIU with exactly zero players with starting experience on the roster for the defense this season. That unit posted respectable numbers in the MAC last year, allowing 24.3 PPG. Defensive coordinator changes and inexperience are also a recipe for trouble. Of the 24 teams that have changed defensive coordinators after a season allowing fewer than 25 PPG and brought back four or fewer defensive starters, only six teams have improved their won-lost percentage. The average decline for the other 18 teams was 26.1% (-3.9 wins) on winning percentage and 13.9% ATS. These teams also covered only 44.4% of their point spreads and allowed 7.9 PPG more. The offense scored just 17.1 PPG, so the fact that five starters are back from that unit with another transferring in may or may not be a blessing. How are they going to keep up with some of the better offenses from the Mountain West? Patience is best preached in circumstances like this, but it’s hard to see more than a win or two this season.

North Texas scored the most points in the country last year, and new head coach Neal Brown was only able to bring in better recruit/ transfer classes than four other programs across the country. Pardon my French, but that is utter failure to start his tenure. The biggest loss is, of course, QB Drew Mestemaker, and replacing him is virtually impossible. There’s a reason oddsmakers have dropped this team’s win total prop significantly coming off a 12-win season. For UNT, the win total figure at DK is 5.5, which of course would represent a drop of 6.5 wins. To answer whether or not the Mean Green will be better or worse, they will undoubtedly be worse. How much worse is the issue. It is backed up by data: 1) Over the last five years, 51 teams have had at least eight fewer returning starters than the prior season, and only 15 of them have improved that season. The average drop-off of those that didn’t improve was a winning percentage decline of 24% (-3.3 wins) and ATS drop of about 6.3%. 2) Teams that are off seasons in which they won 60% or more of their games outright and have 4 or fewer offensive starters returning, plus are breaking in a new quarterback over the last five seasons, have dropped by an average of -3.7 wins, -26% outright, -11.7% ATS, and -6.6 PPG offensively. The eight teams that added a new head coach plummeted by 29% & -4.4 wins per season. Taking a look at the 2026 slate, it could be a difficult three-game start for Brown & Co. with a trip to defending champion Indiana first up. Yikes. Look out below.

Ohio U is another team undergoing massive change for first-year head coach John Hauser, although he was the DC here previously, so perhaps less change than other teams on this Under list. However, teams that are off of seasons in which they won 60% or more of their games outright and have four or fewer offensive starters returning, plus are breaking in a new quarterback, have dropped by an average of -3.7 wins, -26% outright, -11.7% ATS, and -6.6 PPG offensively. The eight teams that added a new head coach plummeted by 29% and -4.4 wins per season. A 4.4-win drop would put the Bobcats at 3.6-8.4. Now, while that may be a bit drastic considering the consistency this program has performed with over the last decade, a drop is expected nonetheless. I think we also need to consider that this team won five of its nine games by seven points or fewer. Radical change can turn that around quickly. Close wins are often characterized as getting “lucky” over the course of a season. Well, teams that have a lot of them and then come back inexperienced are naturally expected to drop. Over the last 13 seasons, 73 teams brought back 14 starters or fewer and had a new QB from a team that was fortunate to get four or more close wins of seven points or fewer in the prior season. Only 11 of these teams finished better the next season, with the average win drop being 2.6 per season, a 16.7% plunge.

In my opinion, there are even varied levels of Stability Scores of zero in college football nowadays. I don’t give negative numbers, but if I did, what Sacramento State and new head coach Alonzo Carter are facing in 2026 would qualify. Not only is he a new coach with a new staff and an almost entirely new roster, but his program is jumping from FCS to FBS and is playing in a conference in a completely different area of the country. And, here’s a weird one for you. As Sacramento State got ready for its final season of FCS- level football a year ago, it scored a program-high 73rd-ranked incoming recruit/transfer class. As it transitions to FBS this year, the class is ranked 122nd. Perhaps potential recruits didn’t like the potential challenges of dealing with a MAC schedule, the Midwest, the mid-week games, etc. As one of the more consistent and high- performing teams from the FCS, the Hornets believe they are ready to compete at the FBS level and in the MAC. The Hornets have won 7+ games in five of the last six seasons of football. That said, there have been 33 teams over the last six seasons that have recorded 4+ blowout wins of 20 points or more one season, then had to change head coaches for one reason or another. Only five of the 33 teams got better the next season, and collectively, they dropped by an average of 17.2%, or 2.8 wins per season, as well as 11.4% ATS. As a group, they were 44.2% ATS. Phil Steele picks them last in the conference, behind even UMass, whose win total is 2.5. Yes, expectations are low.

Recruiting efforts have dropped off severely at San Jose State and third-year head coach Ken Niumatalolo has not been able to revive them. Last year the results finally showed on the field as the Spartans finished 3-9. The incoming talent doesn’t suggest things will get much better in 2026. It seems that Niumatalolo’s coaching magic from his years at Navy has worn off. For this year, he has only three starters back from last year’s 3-9 team, and over the last five years, 51 teams have had at least eight fewer returning starters than the prior season, and only 15 of them have improved that season. The average drop-off of those that didn’t improve was a winning percentage decline of 24% (-3.3 wins) and ATS drop of about 6.3%. SJSU has also changed offensive coordinators, and offensive coordinator changes, when combined with little experience returning, is also a trouble sign. Over the last five seasons, there have been 56 teams that have hired new offensive coordinators the same season they had four or fewer offensive starters returning and a new quarterback. Only 19 teams improved. The 37 teams that did not declined by -17.8% (-2.4 wins) on winning percentages, and -4.1% ATS. They collectively have gone just 45.1% ATS, making them a strong play-against group. The average scoring output dropped about 5.6 PPG. The Spartans can’t afford any drop. This program’s best days might be behind them for a little while.

I am as excited as anyone to see what Brian Hartline can do at South Florida, but I get the feeling that first-year expectations might be a little over-exuberant. Since joining the Ohio State staff in 2017, it was obvious that Hartline was making a beeline for a prominent head coaching spot in college football. As a wide receiver coach and offensive coordinator, his players and teams were among the best in the country. He gets a pretty strong opportunity here, taking over a USF program that made nice strides under Alex Golesh, finishing last season 9-4. It’s a situation that truly looks hard to predict, at least right away. Hartline figures to be successful in short order, and this would then be just a quick hurdle onto a Power Four job. The season win total at 8.5 via DraftKings seems a little aggressive, though. I’ll lean Under, especially since the teams that are off of seasons in which they won 60% or more of their games outright and have four or fewer offensive starters returning, plus are breaking in a new quarterback, have dropped by an average of -3.7 wins, -26% outright, -11.7% ATS, and -6.6 PPG offensively. The eight teams that added a new head coach plummeted by 29% & -4.4 wins per season.

There are 10 teams this season starting with Stability Scores of zero. One of them is Toledo, who, for the last decade or so, has annually been one of the more stable situations year-in and year-out. The Rockets program has been known for having a lot of returning starters each summer, and correspondingly, a lot of success under previous coach Jason Candle. Well, the first domino fell in the spring after Candle’s departure, as the commotion caused was felt in the recruiting results, where replacement Mike Jacobs seems to have taken a big swing and miss in the area of recruiting. To put it simply, Toledo’s 120th ranking from 247Sports is almost a 40-position drop off the 16-year average. Ouch. Jacobs does take over a program that has been in great shape, but there will be some significant challenges this season. The Rockets lost a lot more starts/ experience than they brought in via the transfer portal. Officially, there will only be six players with starting experience back, only two of them Toledo players from the offense. The win total is set at 7.5, and the Rockets are one of only two MAC teams starting the season with new coaching staffs. Still, they are picked first in the conference by many prognosticators. It’s tough to envision this season not being at least a slight decline. I think this prop goes Under. Ken Niumatalolo
